Having applied all three DDM estimation approaches to the same empirical dataset, we can now evaluate a question that is difficult to answer without a unified framework: when do the models agree, and where do approximations break down? Agreement validates the faster models against the gold-standard DDM; disagreement reveals where the computational savings come at a substantive cost.

## Accuracy-Coded Estimates

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison-acc
#| fig-cap: "Cross-model comparison of accuracy-coded parameter estimates. All three estimation approaches (EZ-Diffusion, Censored-Shifted Wald simple, full DDM) converge: emphasis condition clearly affects bound, drift differs strongly across word-frequency levels, and the collapsed word/nonword drift contrast is small in every approach."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "15_cross_model_accuracy.pdf"))
```

@fig-comparison-acc shows the accuracy-coded parameter estimates side by side. All three estimation approaches converge on the same substantive picture: emphasis condition clearly affects bound, drift differs strongly across word-frequency levels, and the collapsed word/nonword drift contrast is small in every approach. This convergence is reassuring — the conclusions hold regardless of whether we use summary statistics (EZ-Diffusion), a single-boundary approximation (Censored-Shifted Wald), or the full Wiener likelihood (DDM).

The approaches diverge in absolute values in ways consistent with their known properties (@tbl-cross-model-acc reports the parameters all three share). The EZ-Diffusion Model produces higher drift estimates than the trial-level approaches — around `r t4_drift_pct_mean`% higher on the frequency scale and more pronounced on the collapsed stimulus-category scale — mirroring the deviation documented in Tutorial 4. For boundary separation, the EZ-Diffusion and Censored-Shifted Wald (simple) estimates agree closely with each other and with the published reference values, while the full DDM estimates somewhat higher boundaries, most visibly under accuracy emphasis, where it draws on the full RT-distribution shape. Non-decision time shows a clear ordering (@tbl-cross-model-acc): the EZ-Diffusion Model estimates higher ndt than the trial-level approaches, likely because it absorbs some decision-time variability that the distributional likelihoods of the full DDM and Censored-Shifted Wald capture directly. These divergences concern the absolute parameter scale. For the questions applied work typically asks — does the manipulation change the parameter, and do individuals differ? — the approaches agree (see Practical Guidelines for this distinction).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cross-model-acc
#| tbl-cap: "Accuracy-coded parameter estimates (posterior mean [95% CrI], natural scale) for the parameters the three approaches share: boundary separation by emphasis condition and non-decision time. Bound and ndt are back-transformed from the log link. Drift is compared in @fig-comparison-acc and @fig-ezdm-vs-ddm."
#| echo: false
.g3 <- function(fe, row, d = 2) fmt_est(exp(fe[row, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), d)
cross_tab_acc <- tibble::tibble(
  Parameter = c("Bound, speed ($\\alpha$)", "Bound, accuracy ($\\alpha$)", "ndt ($\\tau$, s)"),
  `EZ-Diffusion`    = c(.g3(fe_t1,  "bound_conditionspeed"), .g3(fe_t1,  "bound_conditionaccuracy"), .g3(fe_t1,  "ndt_Intercept", 3)),
  `CSWALD (simple)` = c(.g3(fe_t3s, "bound_conditionspeed"), .g3(fe_t3s, "bound_conditionaccuracy"), .g3(fe_t3s, "ndt_Intercept", 3)),
  `Full DDM`        = c(.g3(fe_t4a, "bound_conditionspeed"), .g3(fe_t4a, "bound_conditionaccuracy"), .g3(fe_t4a, "ndt_Intercept", 3))
)
knitr::kable(cross_tab_acc, align = "lccc")
```

## Response-Coded Estimates

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison-resp
#| fig-cap: "Cross-approach comparison of response-coded parameter estimates. Left: Drift estimates by stimulus category — all three approaches show positive drift for words and negative drift for nonwords. Right: Relative starting point by emphasis condition — all three approaches estimate values close to 0.5. The Censored-Shifted Wald (crisk) recovers the same drift sign reversal and near-unbiased starting point as the full DDM; its known underestimation of boundary separation is documented in the text below and the recovery study (Appendix)."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "15_cross_model_response.pdf"))
```

The response-coded comparison (@fig-comparison-resp) evaluates whether the approaches agree on two key patterns: the drift sign reversal by stimulus category and the starting-point shift under speed emphasis. All three approaches recover the expected drift pattern — positive for word stimuli, negative for nonwords — confirming that the response-coding interpretation is robust across estimation approaches. The relative starting point $\zeta$ estimates are close to 0.5 across approaches and emphasis conditions, consistent with the small bias reported in the original @wagenmakers2008lexical analysis. The known bound underestimation of the Censored-Shifted Wald (crisk; see Tutorial 3) is visible in the boundary separation estimates — for boundary-focused questions, the full DDM remains preferable.

## Computational Cost

The fitting time hierarchy — EZ-Diffusion (~30 s), Censored-Shifted Wald (~1–5 h depending on variant), full DDM (~17–21 h) — makes the staged workflow practical. For a typical experiment with 17–30 participants and 200–500 trials per condition, the EZ-Diffusion Model provides results in under a minute that would take the full DDM the better part of a day. For research questions focused on drift, where all approaches agree closely, the EZ-Diffusion Model or Censored-Shifted Wald provide efficient alternatives. When the absolute values of bound or $\zeta$ are central — for example, when estimates are compared against published values — the full DDM is preferable, given the deviations documented above (amplified EZ-Diffusion drift differences, underestimated crisk bound).

# Practical Guidelines

## When to Use Which Approach

The choice among the three estimation approaches (see @tbl-model-comparison) should be guided by the research question and stage of analysis:

- **EZ-Diffusion Model** (`ezdm`): Best for rapid exploration and designs with many conditions. Use 3par by default; 4par when starting-point bias is expected. Requires ~30 trials per cell for stable variance estimates [@lerche2017trials; @lerche2016model].

- **Censored-Shifted Wald** (`cswald`): Recommended for iterative trial-level model development. Use simple for error rates below ~20%, crisk otherwise. Crisk yields DDM-comparable parameters, apart from the bound underestimation noted in Tutorial 3.

- **Full DDM** (`ddm`): Gold standard for confirmatory analysis. Plan for fitting times in the tens of hours (see @tbl-model-comparison).

These recommendations rest on a distinction worth making explicit: what should "accurate estimation" mean in practice? Outside of simulations, the true absolute parameter values are unknown — there is no reference to recover. The criteria that carry applied work are therefore different: an estimation approach must detect differences between experimental conditions or groups, and it must separate individuals reliably [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez]. On both criteria the three approaches converge in our analyses — condition effects replicated across approaches (Cross-Approach Comparison), and subject-level estimates correlated highly with their generating values for all three (Appendix). The absolute-scale biases documented above are, in this sense, primarily a theoretical rather than a practical problem; they matter when estimates are compared against published values or interpreted as measurements on an absolute scale.

## Recommended Workflow

We recommend a staged workflow that exploits the computational hierarchy. This is an efficiency strategy, not a claim that staging produces a better final model: iterating on the predictor structure is cheap with the EZ-Diffusion Model and Censored-Shifted Wald, and — as the cross-approach comparison showed — the faster approaches are trustworthy guides for the drift-focused questions that dominate EAM applications. Divergences that follow the known patterns (amplified EZ-Diffusion drift differences, underestimated crisk bound) are expected by construction; a divergence *beyond* them — a reversed effect, a qualitatively different rank order — signals a potential problem, such as model misspecification or data-quality issues, worth investigating before finalizing the analysis.

1. **Explore with the EZ-Diffusion Model** (`ezdm`): Rapidly screen condition effects on drift and identify which experimental factors influence which parameters.

2. **Develop with the Censored-Shifted Wald** (`cswald`): Transition to `cswald` crisk for iterative development of the trial-level model. Refine the predictor structure, test different random-effects specifications, and evaluate prior sensitivity.

3. **Confirm with the full DDM** (`ddm`): Fit the final model specification using the full DDM likelihood for confirmatory analysis.

4. **Cross-validate**: Compare Censored-Shifted Wald and full DDM estimates as a robustness check.

Throughout all stages, preprocess data using `ezdm_summary_stats(method = "mixture")` for `ezdm` fitting or `flag_contaminant_rts()` for trial-level contaminant detection. Do not apply hard RT cutoffs when using the mixture method.

Adequate trial counts are essential for all approaches (see @tbl-model-comparison). The EZ-Diffusion Model is particularly sensitive because it relies on variance estimates, which stabilize more slowly than means [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion; @lerche2017trials]. For the Censored-Shifted Wald and full DDM, @boag2025expert recommend at least 50 trials per condition for stable hierarchical Bayesian estimation.

## Prior Selection

All tutorials used `bmm`'s default priors — Cauchy(0, 1) on drift, Normal(0, 0.5) on bound (log link), Normal(-1.5, 0.5) on ndt (log link) — which are moderately informative and calibrated for typical data. Defaults can be inspected via `default_prior(formula, data, model)` and overridden using `brms::prior()`:

```{r}
#| label: priors-custom
custom_priors <- prior(normal(0, 2), class = "b", dpar = "drift") +
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b", dpar = "bound")
```

When specifying custom priors, verify that they generate plausible RT data with a prior predictive check — fit with `sample_prior = "only"` and inspect `pp_check()` — and tighten them if the predictions are implausible.

## Common Issues and Troubleshooting

Convergence problems are handled with the standard `brms`/Stan remedies — raise `adapt_delta`, increase iterations, simplify the random-effects structure, or fix $\zeta$ at 0.5; see the `brms` documentation for details [@burkner2017brms]. One issue is EAM-specific: if the Censored-Shifted Wald and full DDM disagree on bound, this is the expected underestimation (see Tutorial 3), not a fitting problem — use the full DDM when boundary separation is the primary research question.

# Summary and Discussion

This tutorial demonstrated three approaches for estimating DDM parameters — the EZ-Diffusion Model, the Censored-Shifted Wald, and full DDM likelihood estimation — applied to empirical data from a classic lexical decision experiment using `bmm`. Three themes emerged: (1) data preprocessing is a quantifiable necessity — the mixture-model approach consistently outperforms hard cutoffs; (2) the three estimation approaches form a useful computational hierarchy for staged analysis; and (3) response coding determines what questions a model can answer — accuracy coding tests selective influence, while response coding reveals decision bias, with practical constraints on the EZ-Diffusion 4par approach when boundary trial counts are unbalanced. Working through the tutorials also delivers on the three objectives set out at the start: readers can now preprocess RT data for contaminant responses (Objective 1); specify, fit, and evaluate DDM-based models with `ezdm`, `cswald`, and `ddm` (Objective 2); and choose among the estimation approaches for a given research question (Objective 3).

## The Hierarchical EZ-Diffusion Model as a Viable Alternative

The cross-approach comparison carries one practical message beyond the staged workflow: for drift-related research questions, the hierarchical EZ-Diffusion Model produced substantively identical conclusions to the full DDM at more than 1,000× lower computational cost (see Tutorial 4). Within `bmm`, the EZ-Diffusion Model is no longer the standalone calculator originally proposed by @wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion but a full Bayesian hierarchical model — with population-level effects, arbitrary predictor structures via `bmf()`, and shrinkage across participants — addressing its two main historical criticisms: contaminant sensitivity (handled by the mixture preprocessing) and the absence of hierarchical structure [@ratcliff2008ez; @vanravenzwaaij2017ez]. Recent work formalizing the EZ-Diffusion equations as a probabilistic proxy likelihood provides the theoretical justification for this use [@chavez2025ez], and prior simulation work reports statistical power for detecting condition effects that is comparable to or higher than the full DDM's [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez] — a literature result we did not re-evaluate, but one consistent with the convergence we observed.

Two qualifications remain. First, clean convergence in sparse cells reflects hierarchical shrinkage: estimates for cells with only a handful of minority-boundary responses are pulled toward the group-level prior and should be read as regularized rather than data-driven. Second, when the research question concerns the shape of the RT distribution (e.g., leading-edge effects, the relative speed of errors) or the absolute values of bound or ndt, the full DDM remains the appropriate choice, with the Censored-Shifted Wald as the trial-level middle ground. For the more common targets — condition effects and individual differences — the estimation biases of the faster approaches are a theoretical rather than a practical concern [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez].

## Limitations

Within the scope defined in the Introduction (simple DDM framework, two-choice tasks), several aspects were not demonstrated. We did not show between-trial variability parameters ($s_v$, $s_\zeta$, $s_\tau$), which can improve fit but create identifiability challenges [@luken2025identifiability; @boag2025expert]; researchers requiring the full seven-parameter DDM should consider alternatives such as HDDM [@wiecki2013hddm] or custom Stan implementations. We also did not cover formal model comparison techniques — bridge sampling and leave-one-out cross-validation are available via `brms` but were beyond the present scope.

## Further Resources

Readers who have completed these tutorials are equipped to estimate DDM parameters from their own two-choice RT data, following the staged workflow in the Practical Guidelines. The `bmm` package also supports mixture models for visual working memory [see @frischkorn2025tutorial for a companion tutorial] and continues to expand. For experimental design guidance, see @boag2025expert; for modeling best practices, @heathcote2015good; for Bayesian data analysis, @mcelreath2020statistical. The `bmm` (<https://venpopov.github.io/bmm/>) and `brms` (<https://paul-buerkner.github.io/brms/>) documentation covers features beyond this tutorial. All data, code, and fitted models are available on OSF (<https://osf.io/XXXXX/>) and GitHub (<https://github.com/GidonFrischkorn/tutorial-ddm-bmm>).

# References

# Appendix: Parameter Recovery on Simulated Data {.appendix}

To verify that the three `bmm` DDM estimation approaches produce reliable estimates, we conducted a parameter recovery study using simulated data with known generating parameters. This complements the empirical tutorials and is consistent with the extensive parameter recovery literature for DDMs [@ratcliff2008diffusion; @vanravenzwaaij2017ez; @lerche2016model].^[The companion script `scripts/21_appendix_parameter_recovery.R` contains the full executable code.]

## Simulation Design

We generated data from a DDM with known parameters (drift: 2.5 for easy, 1.0 for hard; bound: 1.5; ndt: 0.3; $\zeta$: 0.5) for 50 participants, each completing 200 trials per condition. Individual-level parameters were drawn from normal distributions around the population means (see `scripts/20_prepare_simulated_data.R` for details). We then fitted the EZ-Diffusion 3par, Censored-Shifted Wald (crisk), and full DDM to these data following the same `bmm` workflow used in the tutorials. We set two a-priori criteria for successful recovery: at the group level, the 95% credible interval for each parameter should contain its generating value (calibration); at the subject level, true and recovered values should correlate at $r > .70$, the conventional benchmark for treating a measure as a reliable individual-difference index. Of the two, the subject-level criterion is the practically more important one: absolute calibration can only be evaluated in simulations, whereas ordering individuals correctly is what applied uses of DDM parameters — as predictors, covariates, or outcomes — rely on.

## Group-Level Recovery

```{r}
#| label: fig-recovery-group
#| fig-cap: "Group-level parameter recovery. Points indicate posterior means for each estimation approach; error bars show 95% credible intervals. Dashed lines mark the true generating values. All three approaches recover drift and ndt accurately. The Censored-Shifted Wald (crisk) shows the expected underestimation of bound (see Tutorial 3)."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "21_recovery_group.pdf"))
```

All three estimation approaches recovered the generating parameters within their 95% credible intervals (@fig-recovery-group). Drift and ndt estimates were highly consistent across approaches; bound showed the expected crisk underestimation (see Tutorial 3).

## Subject-Level Recovery

Beyond group-level means, we evaluated whether the models recover individual differences by correlating true participant-level parameters with their posterior estimates.

```{r}
#| label: fig-recovery-subject
#| fig-cap: "Subject-level parameter recovery. Each point represents one participant; the x-axis shows the true generating value and the y-axis the recovered posterior mean. High correlations indicate that the estimation approaches preserve the rank ordering of individual differences. Panels show drift (easy condition), bound, and ndt across all three approaches."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "21_recovery_subject.pdf"))
```

Subject-level correlations between true and recovered parameters were high across all estimation approaches (@fig-recovery-subject), ranging from $r$ = `r recovery_r_min` to `r recovery_r_max` (median $r$ = `r recovery_r_median`). These strong correlations indicate that the hierarchical structure in `bmm` preserves individual differences while borrowing strength across participants — an essential property for studies that use DDM parameters as individual difference measures. The results are consistent with published recovery studies and confirm that all three `bmm` estimation approaches produce reliable estimates at both the group and individual level under controlled conditions.
